1.pericope_label: The long war wanes, David’s house grows in Hebron, and Abner makes himself strong for Saul’s house

schools.summary: Ellicott denies pitched battles and describes instead a state of hostility in which each house claimed the allegiance of the whole nation: Ish-bosheth was too weak to carry on actual war, and David was content to abide the fulfilment of the promises of the Lord in his own good time, while time worked in his favour, partly through his rival’s manifest incompetence and partly through a growing realisation that he was the divinely appointed sovereign. Keil and Delitzsch defend the place of the list of sons in the narrative, holding that it does not break the thread, as Clericus and Thenius suppose, but is appropriately introduced as practical proof of the strengthening of David’s house, and that it is in keeping with the custom of opening the history of a reign with notices of the king’s family.

Henry asks why the war was long at all when right and therefore God were on David’s side, and answers that God for wise and holy ends prolonged the conflict, which tried David’s faith and patience and made his establishment at last the more welcome. He then turns the war into a figure of the inward life: the contest between grace and corruption in believers, who are sanctified but in part, may fitly be compared to it, the flesh lusting against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, but as sanctification is carried on, corruption, like the house of Saul, grows weaker and weaker, while grace, like the house of David, grows stronger and stronger, until it comes to a perfect man. On the sons he grants the political effect, every child whose welfare was embarked in the common safety being a fresh security given to the commonwealth, but counts the cost: it was David’s fault to multiply wives contrary to the law and a bad example to his successors, and we read not that any of these sons came to be famous, three being infamous, so that we have reason to rejoice with trembling in the building up of our families. Of the second son he relays what the Hebrew doctors say, that his first name was Daniel, meaning God has judged me, with reference to Nabal, but that David’s enemies said it was Nabal’s son and not David’s, to confute which Providence so ordered it that as he grew he came to resemble David more than any of his children.

Wesley does the arithmetic from the other end, since Ish-bosheth was probably made king at once upon Saul’s death while the other tribes did not submit to David before seven years were expired. He reads one of the marriages as policy, contracted to secure an ally against Ish-bosheth’s party in the north while David opposed him in the south, and judges that he paid dear for making piety give place to policy, as the history of Absalom shows. On the sixth mother he accepts the identification with Michal and explains her being named last by her having been given away to another man.

Gill reckons the war five years longer and supposes it was carried on not in pitched battles, of which we read no more, but in skirmishes. He reports the same etymology of the second son’s name that the Hebrew doctors give but dismisses the story attached to it as a fable not worth relating; and of the sixth mother he notes that she alone is called David’s wife and that the Jews take her for Michal, but objects that Michal had not yet been returned to David in Hebron.

debates.question: How long was the war, and of what kind?

positions.view: No pitched battles at all, but a state of hostility in which each house claimed the allegiance of the whole nation
Five years longer, carried on in skirmishes rather than battles
Ish-bosheth was crowned at once upon Saul’s death, and the tribes did not submit till seven years were expired
Long because God prolonged it for wise and holy ends, to try David’s faith and patience

debates.question: Who is the sixth son’s mother?

positions.view: She alone is called David’s wife and the Jews take her for Michal, but Michal was not yet restored at Hebron
She is Michal, named last because she had been given away to another man
Michal had no child after she mocked David, though she might have had one before

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the long war as a figure of the war between grace and corruption in a believer, and alone in counting David’s growing family a fault as well as a security.
Alone in defending the genealogy’s place in the narrative against Clericus and Thenius.

themes: Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David
But David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker
And unto David were sons born in Hebron
Abner made himself strong for the house of Saul

7.pericope_label: Ish-bosheth’s charge over Rizpah, and Abner’s oath to turn the kingdom to David

schools.summary: Ellicott explains why the charge mattered: an Eastern monarch’s harem was reckoned the property of his successor, so that taking a woman from it asserted a claim to the throne. He thinks it not probable that Abner had any such design, since he was exerting himself to maintain Ish-bosheth, but the king appears to have so regarded the act, and it is that implied charge of treachery which rouses him. On the retort he holds that the received rendering is taken from the Vulgate and is hardly possible, and that it should rather run, am I a dog’s head belonging to Judah? Of the oath he agrees that none is recorded, and suggests that the prophetic declaration that God’s choice of David was unalterable may have been considered to have the force of one. He denies that Abner proposed the change to fulfil the divine will, since his words show he had been acting in conscious opposition to it, and makes revenge the spring of the thing, though he had doubtless also become satisfied of his master’s unfitness, while his power over Israel opened the prospect of high preferment from David; and the suddenness of the resolve suggests he had already had the matter under consideration, which shows there was some ground for the reproach after all. Keil and Delitzsch read the retort the same way, as am I a dog’s head, holding with Judah, and call the figure thoroughly contemptible; of the oath they know none by which God had promised the kingdom to David, but hold the promise of God to be in itself equivalent to an oath, since he can neither lie nor deceive, and observe that the promise was generally known in Israel.

Henry admits that whether the charge was true does not appear, yet suspects Abner guilty because he does not expressly deny it; and he judges it would have been Ish-bosheth’s prudence to be silent, considering how much it was his interest not to disoblige the one man who had ventured all for him. He notices what Abner thinks the service worth, since he magnifies it as rendered against Judah, the tribe on which the crown was settled, so that in supporting Saul’s house he had acted against his conscience and his interest at once; and proud men, he adds, will not bear reproof, least of all from those they think they have obliged. He then watches the man change masters: his ambition had made him zealous for Ish-bosheth and his revenge now makes him as zealous for David, for those who are slaves to their lusts have many masters, driving some one way and some another; yet while Abner serves his own lusts God by him serves his own purposes, and makes even his wrath to praise him.

Gill weighs the charge both ways: if it was false, Abner had reason for his anger; if it was true, he thought he deserved better at such hands than to be reproved for what he might reckon a very small fault.

Clarke turns the oath into an accusation: why did Abner not do this before, when he knew that God had given the kingdom to David, and was he not until now, by his own concession, fighting against God? From the silence that follows the retort he draws a constitutional warning, that miserable is the lot of a king governed by the general of his army, who may strip him of power whenever he pleases, as the fates of Charles the First and Louis the Sixteenth showed; military men, above all others, should never be entrusted with civil power.

debates.question: Was Abner guilty of the charge?

positions.view: Not probable, since he was exerting himself to maintain Ish-bosheth, though the king appears to have so regarded it
Probably guilty, since he does not expressly deny it
Left open: his anger was reasonable if the charge was false, and understandable if it was true

debates.question: What oath of God is Abner swearing by?

positions.view: None is known, but the promise of God is in itself equivalent to an oath, since he can neither lie nor deceive
None is recorded; the prophetic declaration that the choice of David was unalterable may have had the force of one
Whatever it was, Abner knew it, and had therefore been fighting against God by his own concession

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the episode into a constitutional warning about kings governed by their generals.
Alone in reading Abner’s change of side as one lust displacing another while God’s purpose is served by both.

themes: And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah
Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father’s concubine?
Am I a dog’s head, which against Judah do shew kindness this day unto the house of Saul thy father
To translate the kingdom from the house of Saul, and to set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah
And he could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him

12.pericope_label: Abner’s league with David, Michal restored, and the elders of Israel canvassed

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the opening question to mean, to whom does the land belong except to thee. They explain why the demand for Michal went to Ish-bosheth rather than to Abner: that her return might take place in duly legal form, and that it be apparent David had dealt justly with her second husband before his king. The promise Abner urges on the elders they treat as a textual difficulty, holding the verb an evident mistake in writing for a form found in many manuscripts and in all the ancient versions. Ellicott allows either sense of the question but decides for the other, who has power to bring the land into subjection to whom he will except myself, since the question is put as the basis for a league with Abner and accords with the pride and haughtiness of his character, so that he proposes a league to secure consideration for himself and makes it the price of his influence. He counts three political reasons for the demand beside the justice of the claim: it showed all Israel that David bore no malice against the house of Saul, the restoration would again constitute him Saul’s son-in-law and so further his claim, and it showed publicly that he could enforce his rights. Of the promise he agrees it is not contained in so many words in the records we have, and offers two accounts, an unrecorded utterance of one of the prophets, or a reasonable inference from what had been promised and from the divine support of David hitherto.

Wesley reads the opening question as Keil and Delitzsch do, adding that the land is David’s by divine right; and on the canvassing he explains why Benjamin needed separate handling, as the tribe most loath to let the kingdom go out of itself, and so placed between Judah and the rest that winning it would bring in all the others. Clarke puts prudence first in the demand for Michal, that David should not leave a princess in the possession of a man who might in her right have pretended to the throne, besides that she was his lawful wife and he had a right to demand her; yet he gives her second husband the most sympathy of any, since if genuine affection did not still subsist between David and Michal it was a pity to take her from a man who had her to wife by the conjoint authority of her father and her king, though David had a legal right, she having never been divorced but taken from him by violence. Of the promise he asks where it is spoken, answers that such a promise is not extant, and suggests it may mean no more than that thus, it may be presumed, God had determined.

Henry expands the opening question into a speech, that David has the best title to the government and the best interest in the people’s affections. In the demand for Michal he puts the affection first, since neither her marriage nor his own had alienated him from his first and most rightful wife; and he allows her second husband no pity, for though he was loth to part with her and followed her weeping, there was no remedy and he must thank himself, since when he took her he knew another had a right to her, and usurpers must expect to resign. On the promise he supplies the reference the others cannot: when God appointed Samuel to anoint him he did in effect promise that by his hand he would save Israel, for it was to that end he was made king.

debates.question: What does the question Whose is the land? mean?

positions.view: To whom does the land belong except to thee
The same, with the land David’s by divine right
David has the best title to the government and the best interest in the people’s affections
A boast: who but I has power to bring the land into subjection to whom I will? — and so the price of his influence

debates.question: How much is Michal’s second husband owed?

positions.view: Much: it was a pity to take her from a man who held her by the conjoint authority of her father and her king
Sincere attachment, probably returned, yet she was never rightfully his and David’s claim was prior as well as better
None: he knew another had a right to her when he took her, and usurpers must expect to resign

debates.question: Where is the promise Abner cites?

positions.view: Not extant; perhaps it means no more than that thus God may be presumed to have determined
Not in so many words: either an unrecorded prophetic utterance or a fair inference from what had been promised
A textual error, the right form being found in many manuscripts and all the ancient versions
Implied in Samuel’s commission to anoint him, since it was to save Israel that he was made king

outliers.claim: Alone in explaining why Benjamin was canvassed apart from the rest of Israel.
Alone in reading the demand’s being addressed to Ish-bosheth rather than Abner as a point of legal form.

themes: And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, Whose is the land?
Thou shalt not see my face, except thou first bring Michal Saul’s daughter
And her husband went with her along weeping behind her to Bahurim
Ye sought for David in times past to be king over you
And Abner also spake in the ears of Benjamin

22.pericope_label: Joab’s remonstrance, the murder of Abner in the gate, and David’s curse on Joab’s house

schools.summary: Ellicott allows the remonstrance a grain of honesty, thinking it may rest on a genuine suspicion of Abner, for which his long opposition to the divine will and his present revolt gave some ground, but finds personal enmity underneath, partly fear of being supplanted by an older and famous warrior and partly the wish to avenge his brother, so that he seeks to poison David’s mind against him. He reconstructs the murder closely: the gateway was a customary place of conference in the East, so Joab waited there and drew him aside into some place of privacy; the stated reason is the blood of Asahel, but the revenge was no doubt quickened by jealousy. Of the place Abner was recalled from he observes that it is known only from Josephus, twenty stadia from Hebron, so that Abner can only just have left David when Joab arrived. He takes the strength of David’s curse as proof that the act could not be justified as the lawful avenger’s, since Abner had killed Asahel in battle, unwillingly and in self-defence; and he adds the point no one else makes, that Hebron was a city of refuge, where not even the avenger might kill without a trial. He agrees that David remains at fault for keeping Joab in his high position, but attributes it to an inability to punish so powerful a subject, which he sought on his death-bed to remedy by his charge to Solomon. Keil and Delitzsch record only the king’s own protest, that he and his kingdom are innocent before Jehovah for ever of the blood of Abner.

Henry is astonished at the remonstrance: Joab chides his prince and reproaches him to his face as impolitic, as if David were accountable to him, and in effect calls him a fool for trusting a man he knew came to deceive him. I know not whether to wonder more, he says, that Joab had impudence enough to give such an affront or that David had patience enough to take it; and no answer is recorded, not because David feared him as Ish-bosheth had feared Abner, but because he despised him, or because Joab had not manners enough to wait for one. On the plea of blood-vengeance he answers that Abner slew Asahel in open war, after a warning the young man would not take, with reluctance, and in his own defence, whereas Joab shed the blood of war in peace. Of the curse he puts the obvious objection, that a resolute punishment of the murderer himself would better have become David than this passionate imprecation of God’s judgments upon his posterity.

Gill supposes Joab was told of Abner’s visit on entering the palace, so that he came before the king in a passion and flew out again without waiting to be answered. He explains why the curse falls on a house rather than a man: Abishai was in the secret, consenting and advising, and so an accessory, perhaps present and ready to help if needed.

Clarke states the motive flatly, that Joab feared Abner would be made captain of the host and prevented it by murdering him under pretence of avenging his brother; the murder was one of the most unprovoked and wicked, he adds, and the same man served Amasa so a little after, being a cool-blooded and finished murderer. The curse he reads as prediction rather than imprecation, since the verbs may all be rendered in the future, so that it will rest on the head of Joab: a prophetic declaration showing the displeasure of God against this execrable man. Wesley denies the blood-vengeance plea on the same ground as the others, that Abner did it for his own necessary defence, so that it was no justification of this treacherous murder.

positions.view: Fear that Abner would be made captain of the host, carried out under pretence of avenging his brother
Personal enmity — fear of being supplanted and the wish to avenge Asahel — over some genuine suspicion of Abner
Whatever the pretext, he shed the blood of war in peace

debates.question: Was the killing of Asahel a blood-debt Joab might lawfully avenge?

positions.view: No: it was open war, after a warning the young man would not take, with reluctance and in self-defence
No: it was his own necessary defence, and so no justification of this treacherous murder
No: and Hebron was a city of refuge, where not even the avenger might kill without a trial
The curse falls on a house because Abishai was an accessory, consenting and advising

debates.question: Is David’s word a curse or a prophecy?

positions.view: A prediction: the verbs may all be rendered in the future, declaring the displeasure of God against an execrable man
A passionate imprecation, where a resolute punishment of the murderer would better have become him
Proof that the act was indefensible, though David remains at fault for keeping Joab in his place

outliers.claim: Alone in noting that Hebron was a city of refuge, and alone in dating Abner’s departure from the distance Josephus gives for the well of Sirah.
Alone in accounting for the plural reach of the curse by Abishai’s part as accessory.

themes: What hast thou done? behold, Abner came unto thee; why is it that thou hast sent him away
And Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib
I and my kingdom are guiltless before the LORD for ever from the blood of Abner the son of Ner
Let it rest on the head of Joab, and on all his father’s house
So Joab and Abishai his brother slew Abner, because he had slain their brother Asahel

31.pericope_label: The public mourning, David’s lament over Abner, and the king’s plea of weakness

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that David commands the mourning with the usual signs of rent clothes and sackcloth and lays the command especially upon Joab, who is thus required to do public penance for his act, while the king himself follows the bier as chief mourner. He adds the effect, that the people were moved greatly by the sight of David’s sorrow but still more by the elegy, which sums the whole circumstances in a few pregnant words; and of the fast he notes that the people came urging him to eat, but he refused until the sun should be down, the usual hour for ending a fast. Keil and Delitzsch treat the ode as a stronger proof of innocence than either the funeral or the tears, and gloss its key word: the fool is the ungodly man according to Israelitish ideas, so the sense is that Abner had made himself guilty of no crime for which he should die like a malefactor in chains, but had been treacherously murdered. They report the result, that all the people perceived his trouble and were pleased by it, and all Israel discerned that day that the death had not proceeded from the king, as many had probably supposed at first, Joab having fetched Abner back in David’s name.

Henry gives the reason David himself offers for the mourning, that a prince and a great man had fallen that day in Israel, since his alliance to Saul, his place as general, his interest and his former services were enough to denominate him so; and he weighs what the king could honestly say over an enemy, for when David could not call him a saint or a good man he said nothing of that, but gave him the praise of what was true, though Abner had been his enemy.

Gill notices what did not happen, that Joab neither fled nor was laid hold on to be brought to justice, which shows how far he was too hard for David. On the unbound hands and feet he explains that binding is what is done to malefactors taken up and condemned for a crime, which was not Abner’s case, so that had he been aware of the design he might either have defended himself or, finding he had too many to deal with, have used his feet and fled.

Clarke calls the lament short but very pathetic, a high strain of poetry whose measure cannot easily be ascertained; and he takes the plea of weakness at its word, since David had little but the title, one tribe only under his government while the sons of Zeruiah had usurped all the power and reduced him to the shadow of royalty, the doer of evil whose reward he leaves to God being Joab, whom he appears afraid to name. Wesley agrees that Joab was especially obliged to the mourning, to bring him to repentance and expose him to public shame; and though walking after the corpse was against the usage of kings and might seem below David’s dignity, it was now expedient to clear himself of all suspicion of concurrence. He presses the unbound hands and feet against Joab, since Abner did not tamely yield himself to be bound hand and foot, nor did Joab overcome him in equal combat, nor durst he attempt him that way as a soldier of any worth would have done, but by hypocrisy and perfidiousness, whereby the vilest coward may kill the most valiant person. The plea of weakness he allows and then withdraws: it gave some colour to the delay, yet it was a fault that David did not punish them within some reasonable time.

debates.question: What was the public mourning for?

positions.view: Public penance laid especially upon Joab, with the king as chief mourner behind the bier
To bring Joab to repentance and public shame, and to clear David of all suspicion of concurrence
The ode above all, a stronger proof of innocence than either the funeral or the tears
David’s own reason: a prince and a great man was fallen that day in Israel

debates.question: Why dwell on the unbound hands and feet?

positions.view: Binding belongs to a condemned malefactor, which Abner was not; forewarned, he could have fought or fled
Joab did not overcome him in equal combat but by hypocrisy, whereby the vilest coward may kill the most valiant
The fool is the ungodly man, so the sense is that Abner died guilty of no crime deserving a malefactor’s death

debates.question: Is David’s plea of weakness accepted?

positions.view: Yes, at its word: one tribe only, the sons of Zeruiah having usurped all the power and left him the shadow of royalty
It gave some colour to the delay, yet it was a fault that he did not punish them within some reasonable time
The plain fact is that Joab neither fled nor was seized, which shows how far he was too hard for David

outliers.claim: Alone in scanning the lament as verse, and alone in identifying the unnamed doer of evil as Joab, whom David appears afraid to name.
Alone in weighing what David could and could not honestly say in praise of an enemy.

themes: Rend your clothes, and gird you with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner. And king David himself followed the bier
Died Abner as a fool dieth?
Thy hands were not bound, nor thy feet put into fetters
Know ye not that there is a prince and a great man fallen this day in Israel?
And I am this day weak, though anointed king; and these men the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me
